https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwly.text: Figure caption, Watch: RenÃ©e Good's partner speaks publicly for first time since her death By Max Matza Published 1 October 2026 The family of a woman who was killed by an immigration agent in Minneapolis has announced two lawsuits against the US government and members of the Trump administration. Renee Good, a US citizen, was shot to death by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer during a major immigration sweep in January. Millions watched the video recorded of her killing and residents of the Minnesota city took to the streets to protest. One lawsuit blames the government for her death, claiming the operation created "an unprecedented environment for state-sponsored violence", a lawyer for the family said. A White House spokeswoman in a statement called the lawsuits "baseless". The lawsuits were brought by Good's brother, Brent Ganger, and her partner, Becca Good. Speaking publicly for the first time since the shooting, Becca Good told a news conference on the lawsuits on Thursday: "The whole world had to watch as our entire universe was destroyed." "We were all robbed," she said as she described how the shooting affected their three children. In one of the lawsuits, the family accuses the government of "battery, assault, false imprisonment, intentional infliction of emotional distress and negligence that caused Renee's death", according to the family's lawyer. It cites the Federal Tort Claims Act, which allows citizens to sue the government for personal injury, death or property damage caused by the negligence of federal employees. The second lawsuit targets ICE officer Jonathan Ross, who shot Good, as well as White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, White House border tsar Tom Homan and others, alleging a "conspiracy to interfere with civil rights by senior federal officials, federal immigration enforcement agents and private actors". "Our government has become a grave and mortal threat to its own citizens," the family's lawyer, Antonio Romanucci told Thursday's news conference. Image source, Renee Nicole Good Image caption, Renee Nicole Good had recently moved to Minneapolis when she was killed by immigration agents In her statement, Lauren Bis, a spokeswoman for the White House, said the deaths of Americans at the hands of illegal immigrants should merit "equal coverage" by news media. She also said the government will "vigorously defend these baseless civil lawsuits". Trump had initially blamed Good's own actions for her death, saying just hours after she was killed that she "violently, wilfully and viciously ran over the ICE officer". Weeks later, he called her death a "tragedy" and said agents were sometimes "going to make a mistake". The White House also shared a comment from Trump where he said: "I would bet you that she, under normal circumstances, was a very solid, wonderful person - but her actions were pretty tough." He also said ICE agents' work "is being made very difficult" and that "when you look at the way that car was pulled awayâ¦ there are a couple versions of that tape that are very very bad," according to the comments. Good was a 37-year-old mother of three who had just moved to the city. She was shot on 7 January in a traffic stop, which immigration authorities said occurred after she made "an attempt to kill or cause bodily harm to agents". Witnesses disputed that she had been attempting to attack officers. Her death sparked nationwide protests that intensified after another Minneapolis resident, Alex Pretti, was killed by immigration agents on 24 January. Weeks later, hundreds of federal agents were withdrawn from the city and the official in charge of the operation, Greg Bovino, was removed from his post. Granger, Good's brother, said at Thursday's news conference that "since her death no meaningful change has occurred". "Our family is waiting and we will wait no longer," he said. At least 10 people have been killed in encounters with immigration officers during Trump's second term, which began in January 2025, according to the Associated Press. Figure caption, Unpicking the second Minneapolis shooting frame by frame On Tuesday, Good's mother testified at a congressional hearing, saying: "I am a registered Republican. I voted for President Trump under the impression that these agents were here to protect the citizens of the United States. "But far more than being a Republican, I am a Christian," she continued. "Jesus teaches us to forgive and I have, but what we are asking for is accountability." Photograph: Gwent Police./PA Wales Teenage boy stabbed 14-year-old girl 55 times in park in south Wales, jury told Defendant and Lilly Jones had been messaging for months and arranged to meet on evening she was killed, court hears Steven Morris Mon 23 Nov 2026 11.19 EST Last modified on Mon 23 Nov 2026 11.56 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A teenage boy stabbed a 14-year-old girl 55 times after the pair met up in a park near her home, a jury has heard. The body of Lilly Jones was found two days later in a wooded area about 500 metres from her home in south Wales, the court was told. Lilly and the boy, also 14, had been messaging each other for several months having developed “some kind of relationship” and arranged to meet on the evening she was killed, the court heard. Lilly learned the boy was also “in a relationship” with another girl and the two teenage girls had planned to confront him, the jury heard. Anna Pope KC, prosecuting, said: “This case is about the tragic death of Lilly Jones who in June this year had just turned 14. At around 6.30pm on Saturday 20 June she went out, telling her dad she was popping out for a bit. She never came home.” The police were contacted and a missing person investigation began. Lilly was found dead two days after meeting up with the boy, the jury heard, with stab wounds on her neck, back and chest. “The missing person inquiry turned into a murder inquiry,” Pope said. The boy and Lilly were seen on CCTV together at about 6.50pm on the evening she went missing, Newport crown court heard. Pope said: “Police quickly identified that the last person to see Lilly alive was the boy.” When he was first approached by police, the defendant told them he had been due to meet up with Lilly but she did not turn up. After being shown the CCTV footage, he said he had been with her for 15 minutes before he left her, the court heard. Pope said: “We say Lilly did not meet up with anyone else that night. We say that the boy was the last person to see her alive. We say that he was the person who murdered Lilly and then left her in the woods, either dying or already dead.” The court heard the boy and Lilly began to “take an interest” in each other in March when Lilly was 13. Pope said Lilly later learned the boy was also “in some sort of relationship” with another girl. Jurors were told Lilly and the other girl formed a friendship and had planned to confront the boy. The court was told the boy’s DNA was found under Lilly’s nails, from where she had scratched him. A knife was recovered from the boy’s bedroom that could be scientifically linked to Lilly, jurors heard. Her phone was never discovered. Pope said Lilly, from the town of Blaina, enjoyed cosplay, Pokémon and was in regular contact with her friends in school. The prosecutor said Lilly had been shopping with her father for Pokémon cards on the day she was attacked. In opening remarks to the jury, Mrs Justice Stacey said: “The boy says it was not him who did it but it was someone else she met after he left her in the park. The death of a teenage girl, especially in these circumstances, is very distressing, and the fact a 14-year-old boy has been accused of her murder is also very distressing.” The defendant, who cannot be named, denies murder.
